clinicalPearls: It is a descriptive syndrome, not a diagnosis, so always search for reversible contributors before accepting it as end-stage decline.
Four interacting domains dominate: impaired physical function, malnutrition, depression and cognitive impairment.
Depression is among the most common and most treatable drivers, so screen every patient formally.
Polypharmacy and drug side effects such as anorexia, nausea, sedation and postural hypotension are frequently reversible causes.
Exclude occult malignancy, chronic infection such as tuberculosis or endocarditis, thyroid disease and adrenal insufficiency.
Low serum albumin, low cholesterol and lymphopenia are recognised markers of poor prognosis.
Dysphagia, poor dentition, social isolation and financial hardship limiting food access are commonly missed contributors.
Distinguish the syndrome from normal ageing and from an established terminal illness trajectory where the goal shifts to comfort.
reference.pathophysiology: Adult failure to thrive is a multifactorial state of decline in older people characterised by weight loss, reduced appetite, poor nutrition and physical inactivity, often accompanied by dehydration, depressive symptoms and impaired immunity. It represents a final common pathway of accumulated chronic disease, frailty and sarcopenia, driven in part by a pro-inflammatory cytokine milieu with raised interleukin-6 and tumour necrosis factor that promotes catabolism and anorexia. Age-related dysregulation of appetite signalling through leptin and ghrelin, neuroendocrine changes and reduced physiological reserve interact with depression, cognitive impairment and social adversity to accelerate functional and nutritional loss, creating a self-reinforcing cycle of deconditioning.
additionalDifferentials: chronic infection such as tuberculosis or infective endocarditis
advanced cardiac, renal or hepatic failure
additionalInvestigations: cognitive screening and validated depression screening
structured nutritional assessment with albumin and prealbumin
full blood count, urea and electrolytes, calcium and glucose
thyroid function and a morning cortisol
inflammatory markers and targeted malignancy screening or imaging as indicated
redFlags: new focal neurology or lymphadenopathy suggesting malignancy
reference.prognosis: The syndrome carries high morbidity, risk of institutionalisation and mortality, especially when albumin and functional status are low, yet identification and treatment of a reversible cause, particularly depression or a medication effect, can produce meaningful recovery.
pitfalls: accepting decline as inevitable ageing and abandoning the diagnostic workup
failing to assess swallowing, dentition and social or financial barriers to eating
not engaging a multidisciplinary team including dietitian, therapists and social work
references: Brocklehurst's Textbook of Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology
British Geriatrics Society guidance on comprehensive geriatric assessment
management: Identify and treat reversible contributors, particularly depression, trialling an antidepressant where indicated as it is among the most treatable drivers
Review and rationalise medication, stopping agents causing anorexia, nausea, sedation or postural hypotension
Optimise nutrition with dietitian-led assessment, oral nutritional supplementation and treatment of dysphagia or dental problems
Prescribe a structured, progressive exercise and physiotherapy programme to counter sarcopenia and deconditioning
Exclude and treat occult malignancy, chronic infection, thyroid disease and adrenal insufficiency
Undertake comprehensive geriatric assessment coordinating multidisciplinary medical, nursing, occupational therapy and social care input
Address social adversity, cognitive impairment and home safety, arranging appropriate support and placement
Where decline proves irreversible and end-stage, discuss goals of care and consider a palliative approach
